context: fabricate onshore, install offshore · load-out, sail-away and the weather window fix the dates

brief.intro: New to this project type? An offshore platform is built on land and finished at sea. In a fabrication yard, the steel support structure (the jacket) and the deck with all its process equipment (the topsides) are built as large modules, fitted out and tested as far as possible, because every hour of work offshore costs many times more than the same hour onshore. The finished structures are skidded onto barges (load-out), towed to the field (sail-away) and installed by a heavy-lift vessel in a short season when the sea is calm enough. Then the modules are connected, pipelines and risers tied in, and the systems commissioned offshore. The installation vessel is booked years ahead for a fixed window, so the whole project is planned backwards from that date. A floating production unit (FPSO) follows the same idea with a ship hull instead of a jacket.

must_get_right: Plan backwards from the installation window: the heavy-lift vessel is booked for fixed dates, and missing them can cost a year.
Finish and test in the yard. Every incomplete system at sail-away becomes carry-over work offshore; track onshore completion by system, not by percentage.
Control weight from the first day — a module that grows too heavy for the crane or the barge is a schedule problem as much as a design one.
Offshore work is limited by beds and by weather: plan hook-up in man-hours against the accommodation available, with weather downtime included.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Fabrication is organised by structure and module; completion and commissioning are organised by system, onshore and offshore; the installation campaign is a fixed-date block.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Yard calendar with extended shifts; offshore calendar of 12-hour shifts, seven days, with weather downtime allowances by season.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Engineering → steel and equipment delivery → fabrication → equipment, piping, electrical → onshore commissioning by system → load-out → sail-away → installation in the weather window → hook-up → offshore commissioning → first oil. The critical path runs through long-lead equipment into topsides completion before sail-away, then the installation window.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The installation vessel arrives on its contracted dates; weather follows the seasonal statistics; wells and pipelines are ready for start-up at the planned time.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Before equipment installation in the yard

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Weight and space limits on every module; simultaneous trades inside dense modules; offshore beds limit manpower; simultaneous operations with drilling.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: weight growth, late equipment forcing carry-over work, missing the weather window, installation damage, and offshore productivity. Contingency is held before sail-away and inside the installation window.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by module, then system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the yard disciplines and the offshore hook-up crew — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
